text: If the packet is large, you try to protect its transmission by using RTS and CTS, so it is explicit channel reservation. If instead the packet is short, you don't do that, because the other end and the risk that it doesn't work, is not worth it. Okay, it's best to send the packet applying the basic version of the protocol. That's the reason. So you can in a way tune right, how often the RTS and CTS are used or not, by setting these RTS threshold. If you set the RTS threshold to a very high value, then essentially all your packet size will be below and you never use RTS and CTS. If you set the RTS threshold to a lower value, instead, whenever you have a larger packet, larger payload, you are going to use RTS and CTS. So how often actually you apply depends on how you set this configuration parameter called RTS threshold. Now typical values of RTS threshold are 400 bytes or slightly higher than that. Why? Because most of Wi-Fi payloads are 400 bytes or below. So most of them will be transmitted according to the basic scheme. Okay, and only the very large ones will be transmitted using RTS and CTS. However, there are some specific scenarios.
